issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

issues.explanation: The trigger 'my ex' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma and with the rest of the profile, which centers on danger/vigilance cues (blood, temperature, hypervigilance, sleep vigilance, inability to feel safe). This relationship-specific reminder suggests a different interpersonal trauma context that is not represented elsewhere in Threat or other nodes, making the trigger set clinically incoherent for the same index trauma.

vignette: Ahmad, a 29-year-old Middle Eastern male and train conductor, has been struggling with persistent psychological distress since witnessing a traumatic event at work. The incident involved another passenger being severely injured in a collision between two trains. Since that day, Ahmad has found himself acutely sensitive to specific triggers tied directly to the memory of that day. One evening while working his shift, Ahmad felt an unexpected chill on his skin, which immediately transported him back to the traumatic scene. He recalled how the air had suddenly turned cold as he rushed towards the site of the accident. This tactile trigger often leaves him feeling uneasy and hyperalert, convinced that another such event could happen at any moment. His inability to trust others’ assurances of safety only exacerbates his feelings of vulnerability. Visual cues like blood and visible injuries also serve as potent reminders of the traumatic day. During one shift when he encountered a minor accident involving passengers with superficial cuts, Ahmad’s heart raced, and he felt an overwhelming urge to flee from the scene. These visual triggers have made him intensely hypervigilant, always on guard for any sign that could signal another disaster. His constant state of vigilance extends into his personal life as well. At night, Ahmad struggles to fall asleep because he feels he needs to remain alert. This sleep disturbance has left him fatigued and irritable during the day. The weight of these triggers—particularly the tactile sensations and visual cues—keeps him in a heightened state of threat awareness. The specific temperature on his skin that reminds him of the chill from the accident is one such trigger. Each time he feels this sensation, it reinforces his belief that safety cannot be trusted. This reinforcement occurs almost daily during his shifts when environmental changes remind him of the traumatic event. Ahmad's hypervigilance and fear that another disaster could strike at any moment are deeply intertwined with these triggers. For example, a cold wind blowing into the train cabin often sends shivers down his spine and activates his threat response. The sight of blood or visible injuries during his shifts also heightens his anxiety, making him feel that he is constantly in danger. These experiences have become so ingrained in his daily life that he now avoids certain routes on his schedule where incidents are more likely to occur. The cumulative effect of these triggers and their constant activation has taken a toll on Ahmad's ability to function effectively at work. His colleagues notice that he often appears distracted or overly cautious, which has affected team dynamics and even led to some professional disagreements. This heightened state of threat awareness has also strained his personal relationships, as he finds it difficult to fully engage with others without feeling constantly on edge. Despite these challenges, Ahmad's situation finally reached a breaking point when one night, the chill in his home apartment triggered such an intense reaction that he was unable to sleep for several days. This incident pushed him to seek help, recognizing that his quality of life had deteriorated significantly. He is most afraid of another traumatic event occurring and feels deeply uncertain about how to regain trust in his own safety. Ahmad hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to manage his triggers and reduce the constant state of threat awareness that dominates his daily life. His ultimate goal is to reclaim a sense of normalcy and security both at work and at home.
